rv.q: Lyndsey Turner’s production cleverly reframes the story (if you can call it that) in a modern-day care home.
The austerity accentuates the lyrical richness; Thomas’s word-music cuts to the way our identities are bundled up communally with others and our past selves, the living and the dead co-mingled.
It’s an inspired and poignant approach to the piece, the setting acutely topical and quietly assertive of the love and care due to the most fragile in society.

In Lyndsey Turner’s Olivier staging of Under Milk Wood, [Michael Sheen's] galvanising presence and knack for whipping up a storm with words make a strong and emotionally satisfying case for this popular verse drama by Dylan Thomas.

Director Lyndsey Turner fully milks the satirical but tender poignancy of the writing with the aid of a strong, mostly Welsh cast.
Turner’s production hovers in an uneasy place between reading and performance, muddying some of the music and beauty of the text.

Lyndsey Turner’s beautifully timed production is full of delightful cameos.

Turner’s production brilliantly communicates the wit of Under Milk Wood, whether it’s the postman’s wife steaming open everyone’s letters or the murderous fantasies of the put-upon Mr Pugh.

A true, heartening sense of ensemble is sustained, aided in no small part by Michael Sheen as the on-edge son turned ebullient narrator.

And I hadn’t read or heard Under Milk Wood , Dylan Thomas’ play-for-voices, for decades. Actually, not since those cheesy-listening tracks were the grownups’ hip-hop. I remember being thrilled aged eight to find out, against parental intention, that the village of Llareggub whose day the poet relates is a palindrome of “bugger all”.
It's thrilling to see a veteran cast light up the stage and Sheen's passionate narration allows Thomas' poetic prose to soar once more.

cn.t: Michael Sheen delivers a commanding, near-definitive performance in this inventive National Theatre revival, though the framing device of a care home setting divides critics—some find it inspired, others feel it dilutes Dylan Thomas's lyrical masterpiece.
